q: Which compound contains a chiral carbon?
h: A chiral carbon has four different groups attached. Check each C bonded to –OH.
w: In 2-butanol the C–OH carbon carries H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3, all different, so CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 is chiral. 3-Pentanol is not: its C–OH carbon has two identical ethyl groups.

q: How many chiral carbons are in the open-chain form of glucose, CH<sub>2</sub>OH(CHOH)<sub>4</sub>CHO?
h: Check each carbon: the CHO carbon and the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon cannot have four different groups.
w: C1 (CHO) and C6 (CH2OH) are not chiral; C2, C3, C4 and C5 each have four different groups: 4 chiral carbons. Counting C6 or all CHOH and end carbons gives 5 or 6.

q: Which statement about a pair of enantiomers is true?
c: They rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions.
They have different melting and boiling points.
They are superimposable mirror images of each other.
They have different molecular formulas and masses.
h: Enantiomers are mirror images; most physical properties are identical. What is the one optical difference?
w: Enantiomers have the same melting point, boiling point and formula, but rotate polarized light equally in opposite directions. They are NON-superimposable mirror images.

q: Only one enantiomer of many drugs (for example, ibuprofen) is responsible for the drug's effect. Why can enantiomers act differently in the body?
c: Enzymes and receptors are chiral and fit only one enantiomer well.
The two enantiomers have different molecular formulas and masses.
One enantiomer of any chiral drug is always toxic to the body.
Only one enantiomer is soluble enough to dissolve in blood plasma.
h: Think of a right hand fitting into a right-handed glove.
w: Proteins are built from L-amino acids, so their binding sites are chiral and fit one enantiomer better than the other. Enantiomers have the same formula and solubility; one is not automatically toxic.

q: In a Fischer projection, the horizontal lines at a chiral carbon represent bonds that
c: lie in the plane of the page
h: Picture the molecule as a bow tie with the arms reaching out at you.
w: Horizontal bonds come toward the viewer and vertical bonds go back, away from the viewer. The chiral carbon is the intersection of the cross.

q: In the Fischer projection of D-glyceraldehyde, CHO–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>OH, with CHO at the top, the –OH on the chiral carbon is
h: D and L tell which side of the Fischer projection the –OH on the chiral carbon farthest from the C=O points to.
w: In D-glyceraldehyde the –OH points to the right; in L-glyceraldehyde it points to the left.

q: D-Erythrose and D-threose are aldotetroses that differ only in the position of the –OH on carbon 2. These two compounds are
h: They are stereoisomers. Are they mirror images of each other?
w: Only one of two chiral carbons differs, so they are stereoisomers that are not mirror images: diastereomers. Enantiomers would differ at every chiral carbon; constitutional isomers have different bonding.

q: Starting from the Fischer projection of D-glucose, which change gives its enantiomer, L-glucose?
c: Switch the –H and –OH at every chiral carbon.
Switch the –H and –OH at carbon 5 only.
Switch the –H and –OH at carbon 2 only.
Switch the –H and –OH at carbons 2 and 3 only.
h: An enantiomer is the full mirror image. How many chiral centers must change?
w: The mirror image inverts every chiral carbon (C2–C5). Changing only C5 gives a different D/L diastereomer (L-idose), not L-glucose, and changing only C2 gives D-mannose; changing only C2 and C3 gives D-altrose.

q: Ibuprofen is sold as a racemic mixture. What does this mean?
c: It contains equal amounts of two enantiomers.
It contains only the active enantiomer.
It contains equal amounts of two diastereomers.
It contains equal amounts of cis and trans isomers.
h: "Racemic" describes a 50:50 mixture of a particular pair of stereoisomers that are mirror images.
w: A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of a pair of enantiomers, so it contains equal amounts of two enantiomers. Their opposite rotations cancel, so it does not rotate plane-polarized light. Diastereomers are not mirror images.

q: How many chiral carbons are in CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Check each carbon for four different groups. CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub> carbons cannot be chiral.
w: C2 has H, OH, CH3 and the rest of the chain; C3 has H, NH2, CH2CH3 and CH(OH)CH3. Both have four different groups: 2. The CH3 and CH2 carbons have at least two H atoms.

q: How many chiral carbons are in (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?
h: A CH bonded to two CH<sub>3</sub> groups cannot be chiral. Check the carbon bearing –OH carefully.
w: Only the C–OH carbon has four different groups (H, OH, isopropyl, isobutyl): 1. Each CH(CH3)2 carbon carries two identical methyl groups, so it is not chiral, which is the trap behind 3.

q: A chiral carbon is bonded to four different groups. Which compound has a chiral carbon?
h: For each carbon bearing Br, list its four groups. Watch for two identical alkyl groups.
w: In CH3CHBrCH2CH3 the C–Br carbon holds H, Br, CH3 and CH2CH3, all different, so 2-bromobutane is chiral. 3-Bromopentane has two identical ethyl groups, and the other carbons have two or three H atoms or CH3 groups.

q: Threonine, an essential amino acid, is CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)COOH. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: Check each carbon: CH<sub>3</sub> and –COOH carbons cannot be chiral. Look at the two CH carbons.
w: The CH(OH) carbon holds H, OH, CH3 and CH(NH2)COOH; the CH(NH2) carbon holds H, NH2, COOH and CH(OH)CH3. Both have four different groups: 2 chiral carbons.

q: D-Glucose and D-galactose have the same formula and differ only in the arrangement at carbon 4 (one of their several chiral carbons). They are
h: Enantiomers are opposite at EVERY chiral carbon. What do you call stereoisomers that differ at only some of them?
w: Same connections, different 3-D arrangement at only one of several chiral carbons, and not mirror images: diastereomers. Enantiomers (like D- and L-glucose) are opposite at every chiral carbon.

q: Ribose, the sugar in RNA, has 3 chiral carbons in its open-chain form. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers possible?
h: Each chiral carbon has two possible arrangements. Multiply the possibilities.
w: Maximum stereoisomers = 2n = 23 = 8. Those 8 are four pairs of enantiomers, so 4 counts the pairs instead of the compounds; 6 comes from 2 × 3 and 3 from counting the chiral carbons themselves.

q: How many chiral carbons are in the pain reliever ibuprofen, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COOH (the ring is a para-disubstituted benzene)?
h: Benzene ring carbons, CH<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub> and COOH carbons are not chiral. Check the two CH carbons.
w: The CH in (CH3)2CH– has two identical CH3 groups, so it is not chiral. The CH(CH3)COOH carbon holds H, CH3, COOH and the ring: chiral. Total = 1.

q: A chiral molecule (not meso) has exactly two chiral carbons. In a wedge-and-dash drawing, you swap two groups on BOTH chiral carbons. The new structure is
c: a constitutional isomer of the original
h: Swapping two groups on one chiral carbon inverts that center. What is the relationship when every center is inverted?
w: Each swap inverts one chiral carbon. Inverting both (all) chiral carbons gives the mirror image, and because the molecule is chiral, that mirror image is the enantiomer. (For a meso compound the mirror image is the same compound, which is why the stem says the molecule is chiral.) Inverting only one of the two would give a diastereomer; connectivity never changes, so it is not a constitutional isomer.

q: Menthol, shown, gives mint toothpaste and cough drops their cooling feel. How many chiral carbons does menthol have?
h: A chiral carbon has four different groups. In a ring, compare the two paths around the ring from that carbon.
w: The ring carbons bearing the OH, the methyl group and the isopropyl group each have four different groups (H, the substituent and two ring paths that are not the same), so menthol has 3 chiral carbons. CH2 ring carbons and the isopropyl CH (two identical CH3 groups) are not chiral.

q: Ibuprofen, shown, is a common pain reliever. How many chiral carbons does it contain?
h: Check each carbon with four single bonds that has one H: does it have four different groups? Carbons in the benzene ring and CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>2</sub> groups never qualify.
w: Only the carbon next to the COOH group has four different groups: H, CH3, COOH and the ring, so there is 1 chiral carbon. The CH in the isobutyl group carries two identical CH3 groups, so it is not chiral; ring carbons have only three groups.

q: Ibuprofen is shown with four carbons labeled. Which labeled carbon is a chiral carbon?
h: A chiral carbon has four different groups. Carbons with a double bond, or with two identical groups, cannot be chiral.
w: Carbon b carries H, CH3, –COOH and the benzene ring: four different groups, so it is chiral. Carbon d is the tempting wrong answer, but it carries two identical CH3 groups. Carbon a (in the ring) and carbon c (the C=O carbon) have a double bond, so they have only three groups.

q: Carvone, shown, gives spearmint its smell; its mirror image smells like caraway. Which labeled carbon is the chiral carbon?
h: In a ring, compare the two paths around the ring from each carbon. Are they the same?
w: Carbon c has H, the isopropenyl group and two different ring paths (one toward the C=O, one toward the C=C), so it is chiral. Carbon d is a CH2 (two identical H atoms). Carbon a (ring C=C) and carbon b (the C=C of the side chain) each have a double bond, so neither has four groups.

q: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed), shown, is a nasal decongestant. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: Check every carbon with one H and no double bond. Does each have four different groups?
w: The carbon bearing the –OH (H, OH, ring, rest of chain) and the carbon bearing the N (H, CH3, NHCH3, rest of chain) each have four different groups: 2 chiral carbons. Ring carbons have a double bond, and the CH3 carbons have three identical H atoms. Answering 1 usually means the C–N carbon was missed.

q: The open-chain form of fructose (fruit sugar) is shown. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: End carbons (CH<sub>2</sub>OH) have two identical H atoms, and the C=O carbon has a double bond. Check the rest.
w: Fructose has six carbons. The two CH2OH carbons have two H atoms each, and the ketone carbon (C=O) has only three groups, so they are not chiral. The 3 CH(OH) carbons in between each have four different groups. Answering 4 is the count for glucose, an aldose with four CH(OH) carbons; 6 counts every carbon.

q: Which molecule shown is chiral?
h: Look for a carbon with four different groups: H, and three different non-H groups.
w: Lactic acid has a carbon bonded to H, CH3, OH and COOH: four different groups, so the molecule is chiral. Glycerol is the tempting wrong answer: its middle carbon has H and OH but two identical –CH2OH groups. Glycine's CH2 has two H atoms, and 2-propanol has two identical CH3 groups.

q: Which molecule shown is achiral (has no chiral carbon)?
h: For the carbon bearing the OH, NH<sub>2</sub> or Cl, are the two carbon groups attached to it the same or different?
w: In 3-pentanol the C–OH carbon has H, OH and two identical ethyl groups, so it is not chiral. In 2-pentanol the two carbon groups differ (CH3 vs propyl), so it is chiral; alanine and 2-chlorobutane each also have one chiral carbon. Having an OH on a middle carbon does not by itself make a carbon chiral.

q: Thalidomide, shown, was given to pregnant women in the late 1950s; one mirror-image form eased morning sickness, while the other caused severe birth defects. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: Ignore carbons with double bonds (C=O, ring C=C) and CH<sub>2</sub> groups. What is left?
w: Only the ring carbon bonded to H, the N of the other ring system, a C=O carbon and a CH2 has four different groups: 1 chiral carbon. All the C=O and benzene carbons have double bonds, and the two CH2 carbons have two H atoms each. Even one chiral carbon is enough to give two mirror-image forms.

q: Alanine, shown, has one chiral carbon, so it exists in two forms that are nonsuperimposable mirror images of each other. What are these two forms called?
h: Think of left and right hands: mirror images that cannot be stacked on top of each other.
w: Two nonsuperimposable mirror images are enantiomers (like L- and D-alanine). Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images; for chiral-carbon compounds that takes at least two chiral carbons. Structural isomers have different connections between atoms, and cis–trans isomers come from a C=C or a ring, not from a chiral carbon.

q: Epinephrine (adrenaline), shown, is the drug in an EpiPen. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: Check each carbon in the side chain. A CH<sub>2</sub> has two identical H atoms; ring carbons have a double bond.
w: Only the carbon bonded to the –OH has four different groups (H, OH, the ring and CH2NHCH3): 1 chiral carbon. The tempting answer 2 counts the CH2 next to N, but it has two H atoms. Ring carbons and the N-methyl carbon are not chiral, and N atoms are not counted as chiral carbons.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Compare each chiral carbon. Are both wedges/dashes switched, or only one? Then ask whether the molecule has an internal mirror plane.
w: Both wedge/dash bonds are switched, so II is the mirror image of I. This form of 2,3-butanediol has no internal mirror plane, so the mirror image is not superimposable: enantiomers. Compare the meso form, where switching both gives the same compound.

q: What is the relationship between molecules I and II?
h: Switching every wedge and dash draws the mirror image. But is this molecule chiral? Compare the three groups on each chiral carbon.
w: Switching both wedge/dash bonds draws the mirror image. But this is meso-2,3-butanediol: the two halves (CH3, H, OH on each chiral carbon) mirror each other, so the molecule is achiral and its mirror image is the same molecule. I and II are identical (same compound), not enantiomers.

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: Look at each chiral carbon in turn. How many of the two have a different wedge/dash in II than in I?
w: Only one of the two chiral carbons is different (one dash became a wedge). Stereoisomers that differ at some, but not all, chiral carbons are diastereomers, not mirror images. Here I is the meso form and II is one of the chiral forms of 2,3-butanediol.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Picture turning drawing I like a steering wheel, keeping it flat on the page. Do wedges stay wedges?
w: II is just I turned 180° in the plane of the page. Turning a drawing on the page never changes a wedge into a dash, so every group keeps its front/back position: identical (same compound). Students who see the groups on "opposite sides" often call these enantiomers.

q: What is the relationship between molecules I and II?
h: Imagine a mirror standing between I and II. Is II exactly the reflection of I? Then ask: is I superimposable on its reflection?
w: II is the reflection of I in a vertical mirror: the left–right layout is reversed and the wedges stay wedges. This form of 2,3-dibromobutane has no internal mirror plane, so the reflection is not superimposable: enantiomers.

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: Count how many chiral carbons are switched. Could this molecule be meso when one carbon has Br and the other has Cl?
w: Both wedge/dash bonds are switched, which gives the mirror image. 2-Bromo-3-chlorobutane cannot be meso, because its two chiral carbons carry different groups (Br vs Cl), so no internal mirror plane exists: enantiomers.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Check the carbon with Br, then the carbon with Cl. Which ones changed between wedge and dash?
w: The carbon bearing Br is the same in both drawings; only the carbon bearing Cl is switched. Changing one of two chiral carbons gives a stereoisomer that is not a mirror image: diastereomers.

q: What is the relationship between molecules I and II?
h: Flipping a molecule over like a pancake reverses left–right AND turns every wedge into a dash. Does II match I after a flip?
w: II looks like a mirror image because left and right are reversed, but every wedge has also become a dash. That is exactly what you see after turning the molecule over (a 180° turn out of the page), so I and II are identical (same compound). A true mirror image would reverse the layout but keep the wedges.

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: First turn II by 180° in the page so the OH carbon is on the same side as in I. Then compare each chiral carbon.
w: Turn II 180° in the plane (wedges stay wedges) so it lines up with I. The carbon with OH now matches, but the carbon with Cl has the opposite wedge/dash. One of two chiral carbons is different: diastereomers.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Both methyls change between wedge and dash. Is this ring compound cis or trans, and does it have an internal mirror plane?
w: In I one methyl is a wedge and one is a dash (trans); in II both are switched. The trans isomer has no internal mirror plane, so switching both chiral carbons gives a non-superimposable mirror image: enantiomers.

q: What is the relationship between molecules I and II?
h: Both methyls are on the same side of the ring in each drawing. Does the cis compound have an internal mirror plane?
w: Both drawings are cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane: methyls both toward you in I and both away in II. Flip I over and you get II. The cis compound is meso (a mirror plane cuts between the two chiral carbons), so I and II are identical (same compound).

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: Decide whether each drawing has the methyls on the same side of the ring or on opposite sides. Then count how many chiral carbons differ.
w: I is cis (both wedges) and II is trans (one wedge, one dash). Cis and trans ring isomers have the same connections but are not mirror images, so they are diastereomers (they even have different boiling points).

q: What is the relationship between molecules I and II?
h: Both OH groups are on the same side of the ring in each drawing. Is cis-1,3-cyclopentanediol chiral, or does it have an internal mirror plane?
w: Both drawings show the two OH groups on the same side of the ring (cis): toward you in I, away in II, and II is also turned on the page. cis-1,3-Cyclopentanediol has a mirror plane through C2 and the middle of the opposite C–C bond, so it is meso and I and II are identical (same compound).

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: Turn II in the plane so its OH groups line up with I. Then compare wedges: is each one switched, or only one?
w: Both are trans (one OH wedge, one dash). After turning II 180° in the page, each OH sits where it does in I but with the opposite wedge/dash. Both chiral carbons are switched and trans-1,2-cyclopentanediol has no mirror plane, so they are enantiomers.

q: Structure I is threonine, an amino acid found in proteins. How are I and II related?
h: Compare the carbon bearing NH<sub>2</sub> and the carbon bearing OH separately. How many changed?
w: The carbon with NH2 is the same in I and II; only the carbon with OH is switched. One of two chiral carbons different means diastereomers. (I is threonine, the amino acid in proteins; II is allothreonine.)

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: Turn II 180° on the page so COOH points the same way as in I. Then compare both chiral carbons.
w: After turning II 180° in the plane (wedges stay wedges), it lines up atom for atom with I, but both the NH2 and the OH have the opposite wedge/dash. Both chiral carbons switched, no mirror plane: enantiomers. II is the mirror-image form of threonine, which the body cannot use in proteins.

q: Ephedrine (I) and pseudoephedrine (II, the decongestant in Sudafed) are shown. How are they related?
h: Both drugs have two chiral carbons. Compare the carbon with OH and the carbon with the N group one at a time.
w: The carbon with the NHCH3 group is the same in both; only the carbon with OH is switched. One of two chiral carbons different: diastereomers. That is why the two drugs have different melting points and different effects in the body.

q: Two four-carbon sugars, I and II, are drawn as zig-zag chains. How are they related?
h: These four-carbon sugars have two chiral carbons. Compare the OH next to the CHO, then the other OH.
w: Only the OH on the carbon next to the CHO is switched; the other chiral carbon is unchanged. One of two chiral carbons different: diastereomers (I is erythrose, II is threose). For enantiomers, both OH groups would have to switch.

q: Which structure is the enantiomer of the molecule shown?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: The enantiomer has both chiral carbons switched (each wedge ↔ dash, same layout). Switching only one gives a diastereomer. The drawing turned 180° on the page is the same compound, and the one with Br on the end carbon is a constitutional isomer.

q: Which structure is the enantiomer of the molecule shown?
h: Imagine a mirror beside the molecule: the reflection reverses left and right but keeps wedges as wedges.
w: A mirror beside the molecule reverses left and right but keeps wedges as wedges: that reflection is the enantiomer. The tempting choice that is reversed left–right AND has every wedge switched is just the molecule flipped over, so it is the same compound. Switching one center gives a diastereomer; moving Cl to the end carbon gives a constitutional isomer.

q: Which structure is the enantiomer of the molecule shown?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: The enantiomer keeps the trans arrangement but switches both methyls (wedge ↔ dash). The cis drawing (both wedges) is a diastereomer; the drawing turned 180° on the page is the same compound; and the 1,3-dimethyl ring is a constitutional isomer.

q: Threonine, an amino acid, is shown. Which structure is its enantiomer?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: Turn each choice so COOH points the same way as in threonine. The enantiomer (drawn turned 180°) has both NH2 and OH switched. The one with only OH switched is a diastereomer (allothreonine). The left–right reversed drawing with all wedges switched is threonine flipped over; swapping where NH2 and OH are attached gives a constitutional isomer.

q: Which structure is the enantiomer of the molecule shown?
h: The enantiomer is the mirror reflection. Check that the ring compound stays trans and the OH groups stay on neighboring carbons.
w: Reflecting the molecule in a vertical mirror reverses left and right and keeps each wedge or dash: that is the enantiomer (still trans). The cis diol is a diastereomer, the drawing turned 180° on the page is the same compound, and the 1,3-diol is a constitutional isomer.

q: Ephedrine, a drug used to raise blood pressure, is shown. Which structure is its enantiomer?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: The enantiomer has both chiral carbons switched (OH and the CH3/NH group). Switching only the OH carbon gives pseudoephedrine, a diastereomer. The drawing turned 180° on the page is ephedrine itself; swapping where OH and NHCH3 are attached is a constitutional isomer.

q: The sugar erythrose is shown. Which structure is its enantiomer?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: The enantiomer switches both OH groups on the chiral carbons. Switching just one gives threose, a diastereomer. The 180°-turned drawing is erythrose itself, and the ketone (C=O in the middle) is erythrulose, a constitutional isomer.

q: Which compound is a meso compound?
h: A meso compound has chiral carbons but an internal mirror plane: the two halves must carry identical groups and mirror each other.
w: In meso-2,3-dibromobutane the two halves are identical (CH3, H, Br) and arranged as mirror images, so an internal mirror plane makes the molecule achiral: meso. The other 2,3-dibromobutane drawing has no mirror plane. 2-Bromo-3-chlorobutane cannot be meso (Br ≠ Cl), and trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane is chiral.

q: Which molecule is achiral even though it has chiral carbons?
h: You need a molecule that HAS chiral carbons and also has an internal mirror plane. Watch for a molecule with no chiral carbons at all.
w: cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane has two chiral carbons, but a mirror plane runs between them, so it is achiral: a meso compound. Trans is chiral, and 2-methylcyclohexanol cannot be meso (CH3 ≠ OH). Methylcyclohexane is achiral but has no chiral carbon, so it does not fit the question.

q: Which of these five-membered ring compounds is a meso compound?
h: Look for two chiral carbons with identical groups on the same side of the ring, arranged so the ring can be cut into mirror-image halves.
w: cis-1,3-Cyclopentanediol (both OH wedges) has a mirror plane through C2 and the middle of the opposite C–C bond, so it is meso. The trans diols (one wedge, one dash) are chiral. Cyclopentanol is achiral but has no chiral carbon, so it is not meso.

q: Tartaric acid is found in grapes and is used in baking powder. Which drawing shows meso-tartaric acid?
h: Both chiral carbons carry H, OH and COOH. Which arrangement lets one half be the mirror image of the other?
w: In meso-tartaric acid the two halves (H, OH, COOH on each chiral carbon) mirror each other, so the molecule has an internal mirror plane and is achiral. The other two tartaric acid drawings are the pair of chiral enantiomers. Malic acid (only one chiral carbon) is chiral.

q: Erythritol, the zero-calorie sweetener shown, has two chiral carbons. Which statement about erythritol is true?
c: It is achiral because it has an internal mirror plane (meso).
It is chiral because it contains chiral carbons.
Its mirror image is a different compound (an enantiomer).
It has four possible stereoisomers in total.
h: Look at the two halves of the molecule. Are the groups on each chiral carbon identical, and are they arranged as mirror images?
w: Both chiral carbons carry H, OH and CH2OH, and here they are arranged as mirror images, so erythritol has an internal mirror plane: achiral (meso). Having chiral carbons does not guarantee a chiral molecule. Because of the meso form, this formula has only 3 stereoisomers, not 22 = 4.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for 2,3-butanediol, shown?
h: Count chiral carbons (n) to get the maximum 2<sup>n</sup>. Then check whether one combination has an internal mirror plane (meso).
w: There are 2 chiral carbons, so at most 22 = 4. But the two halves are identical (CH3, H, OH), so the two "mixed" combinations are one and the same meso compound. Total: a pair of enantiomers + 1 meso = 3, not 4.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane, shown?
h: Count the chiral carbons and use 2<sup>n</sup>. Could a meso form exist when the two chiral carbons carry different groups?
w: 2 chiral carbons give 22 = 4 stereoisomers (two pairs of enantiomers). Unlike 2,3-butanediol, no meso form is possible, because one chiral carbon has Br and the other has Cl, so no internal mirror plane can exist.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, shown?
h: Two chiral ring carbons give at most 2<sup>2</sup>. Is the cis form (both methyls on the same side) chiral or meso?
w: The 2 chiral carbons allow at most 22 = 4. The trans form exists as a pair of enantiomers, but the cis form has a mirror plane (meso), so its "two" drawings are the same compound. Total: 3.

q: Tartaric acid, shown, is the sour acid in grapes. How many stereoisomers of tartaric acid are possible?
h: Count the chiral carbons, apply 2<sup>n</sup>, then ask whether the two identical halves allow a meso form.
w: 2 chiral carbons give at most 22 = 4. The two halves are identical (H, OH, COOH), so one combination is meso and is counted once. Tartaric acid has 3 stereoisomers: two enantiomers plus meso-tartaric acid.

q: Threonine, an essential amino acid, is shown. How many stereoisomers of threonine are possible?
h: Find every carbon with four different groups, then use 2<sup>n</sup>. Check whether a meso form is possible.
w: Threonine has 2 chiral carbons (the one with NH2 and the one with OH), so 22 = 4. The two chiral carbons carry different groups, so there is no meso form; the four are two pairs of enantiomers, and only one is used in proteins.

q: Carvone I smells like spearmint, and its mirror image II smells like caraway (rye bread). Which property is different for I and II?
c: The direction they rotate plane-polarized light
Their boiling points at the same pressure
Their densities as pure liquids at 25 °C
h: I and II are enantiomers. Which properties depend on "handedness"? Only interactions with something chiral, or with polarized light, can tell them apart.
w: I and II are mirror images (enantiomers). Enantiomers have identical boiling points, densities and solubility in ordinary solvents, but they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions (by the same amount). They also smell different because the smell receptors in your nose are chiral.

q: A pure sample of the caraway form of carvone rotates plane-polarized light by +61°. Measured the same way (same concentration and tube), what rotation does the pure spearmint form, its enantiomer, give?
h: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by the same amount but in opposite directions.
w: Enantiomers rotate light by equal amounts in opposite directions, so the spearmint form gives −61°. 0° would be a 50:50 (racemic) mixture of the two, and +61° would mean the sample is the caraway form itself.

q: The two enantiomers of the pain reliever ibuprofen, I and II, are shown. Which property is the same for pure I and pure II?
c: Direction of rotation of plane-polarized light
How well each fits the pain-related enzyme it blocks
h: Enantiomers behave alike toward anything that is not chiral, but differently toward polarized light and chiral enzymes.
w: Enantiomers have identical physical properties such as melting point, boiling point and solubility. They rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions, and because enzymes are chiral, only one form (the active one) fits the enzyme well, so their pain-relieving power differs.

q: The two mirror-image forms of thalidomide cannot be separated by distillation or by dissolving one in water. Why not?
c: Enantiomers have identical boiling points and identical solubility in water.
Enantiomers have different boiling points, but both decompose when heated.
Diastereomers like these always form a racemic mixture.
The two forms are constitutional isomers with the same molecular mass.
h: Distillation separates by boiling point; dissolving separates by solubility. How do these properties compare for mirror-image molecules?
w: Mirror-image forms (enantiomers) have identical boiling points and solubility in ordinary (achiral) solvents, so distillation and simple dissolving cannot separate them. Separating enantiomers needs something chiral, such as a chiral column. The two forms are enantiomers, not diastereomers or constitutional isomers.

q: L-DOPA, shown, treats Parkinson's disease; its enantiomer, D-DOPA, does not work in the body. A pharmacist has a pure sample of each. Which measurement can tell them apart?
c: The direction each rotates plane-polarized light
The melting point of each pure solid sample
The solubility of each in water at 25 °C
The molar mass of each, from its formula
h: Enantiomers share nearly every physical property. Which measurement uses something "handed" that can sense the difference?
w: L- and D-DOPA are enantiomers: same melting point, same solubility, same molar mass. A polarimeter tells them apart because the two forms rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions. The body also tells them apart, because its enzymes are chiral.

q: Ephedrine (I) and pseudoephedrine (II) melt at very different temperatures. Which statement explains this?
c: They are diastereomers, and diastereomers can have different physical properties.
They are enantiomers, and enantiomers have different melting points.
They are constitutional isomers with different molecular formulas.
They are the same compound, so the difference must come from impurities.
h: Compare the two chiral carbons. Are both switched, or only one? Then recall which kind of stereoisomer has different physical properties.
w: Only the carbon with OH is switched, so I and II are stereoisomers that are not mirror images: diastereomers. Diastereomers have different shapes overall, so their melting points, boiling points and solubilities differ. Enantiomers would have identical melting points; constitutional isomers have the same formula, not different ones.

q: In the drawing of 2-butanol shown, the OH is attached by a solid wedge. What does the wedge tell you about the OH?
c: It points toward the viewer, out of the page.
It points away from the viewer, behind the page.
It lies flat in the plane of the page.
It is joined by a stronger bond than a plain line.
h: Plain lines lie in the page. One kind of stereo bond comes toward you; the other goes behind the page.
w: A solid wedge means the group points toward the viewer, out of the page (the wide end is nearer to you). A hashed (dashed) wedge means the group points away, behind the page. Plain lines lie in the plane of the page. The wedge says nothing about bond strength.

q: In the 2-bromobutane drawing shown, the Br is on a dashed bond (behind the page). If you redraw it with the Br on a solid wedge and change nothing else, what do you get?
c: A constitutional isomer of the original
h: The molecule has only one chiral carbon. What does switching the only chiral carbon do?
w: Moving Br from behind the page to in front switches the only chiral carbon, which produces the non-superimposable mirror image: the enantiomer. With only one chiral carbon, a diastereomer is impossible; diastereomers need at least two chiral carbons.

q: 3-Chloro-2-butanol is shown. If you switch the wedge/dash on the carbon bearing Cl only, and leave the OH carbon unchanged, what is the new structure?
c: A constitutional isomer of the original
h: The molecule has two chiral carbons. An enantiomer needs every chiral carbon switched. How many did you switch?
w: Switching one of the two chiral carbons gives a stereoisomer that is not the mirror image: a diastereomer. To get the enantiomer you would have to switch both the Cl carbon and the OH carbon. Connections are unchanged, so it is not a constitutional isomer.

q: The drawing of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane shown is turned 180° in the plane of the page (like turning a steering wheel). The turned drawing shows
h: When a drawing turns flat on the page, does a group in front of the page end up behind it?
w: Turning a drawing within the plane of the page moves groups around on the page but never moves anything from front to back, so every wedge stays a wedge and every dash a dash: the same compound. Only a reflection, or switching every wedge and dash, gives the enantiomer.
